How easy is it for you to make it use tip tap instead plain textarea to edit the contents, tip tap with drag and droppable images and a video component a link to youtube becomes a video

Easy on the editor, one real decision on the images.

**The editor itself.** Tiptap fits the shape we have. It runs on Vue 3.5 and Vite 4, and the ivue standard absorbs it cleanly: one `EditorModel` class owns the Tiptap instance the way the Lenis fork owns its scroller, created in the constructor, destroyed on unmount, every command a method. With `tiptap-markdown` it reads and writes the markdown subset the press already stores, so the Worker, the lint, the projections and the poster do not change. Images serialize to `![alt](url)`, a YouTube link stays a link in the markdown, and the preview and the Tiptap document both render it as the embedded player through `@tiptap/extension-youtube`. Storage stays one format. That is about a day: the base editor plus the split editors for articles, Reddit, dev.to and the HN comment, with a small toolbar, drag-and-drop and paste of images, and the YouTube node.

**Where it should not go.** X tweets, LinkedIn posts, Bluesky, Mastodon and email are plain text on the platform, so their cards keep the plain contenteditable. Rich formatting there would only be stripped by the lint. What those cards do deserve is image drops: X segments already carry `meta.imageUrls` and the poster attaches them, so a drop zone per tweet closes the loop from drag to posted image.

**The decision: where dropped images live.** Today every image is site-hosted under `docs_v2/public`, committed and deployed. A drop in the editor needs a store the Worker can write to and X can read from by public URL. The natural answer is an R2 bucket bound to the Worker, one `POST /admin/press/asset` route, files served under a public path. That is an hour of Worker work plus a wrangler binding you create once. Without it, drag-and-drop can only accept URLs, not files.

**Video beyond YouTube.** A YouTube link becomes a player in the base, the articles and the previews. X itself has no YouTube embed: a link in a tweet becomes a link card, and native video means uploading the file through the X media API, which the poster does not do yet. If you want video in tweets, that is a separate piece: R2 upload plus chunked media upload to X, half a day.

So: editor and YouTube, one day, no new infrastructure. Image drops, add R2 and an hour. Native video on X, a further half day. Say which of the three and I'll start.

Is r2 bucket free

Yes for this use. R2 has a permanent free tier, not a trial: 10 GB of storage, 1 million write-class operations and 10 million read-class operations a month, and egress is free at any volume. There is no charge for bandwidth out, which is the part that makes other object stores expensive.

For press images that is effectively unlimited. A launch quarter of a few hundred images at a megabyte each sits at a few hundred megabytes of storage and a few thousand writes. Reads are the public fetches, and even a viral post's traffic stays far under 10 million.

Two practical notes:

- **Public access** is what the poster needs, and it is free too. You either enable the bucket's public URL, or, cleaner and what I would do, serve the objects through a route on the Worker you already have, which keeps the URLs on your domain and lets the admin secret gate the uploads while reads stay open.
- **Creating the bucket** is a one-time step on your side, `wrangler r2 bucket create ivue-press`, then a binding in `wrangler.jsonc`. Wrangler needs the R2 subscription enabled on the account, which is a click in the dashboard and costs nothing until you pass the free tier.

The pricing beyond the tier is fifteen cents per GB-month of storage and a few dollars per million operations, so even a mistake would be cents.

parts.text:
Everything I need is measured. Here is the full picture.

**What resolveRaw does.** Every engine entry point (method getter and setter, ref-getter, de-opted getter and setter, `$watch`, `$watchEffect`, `$stopEffects`) receives `this` as whatever the caller held, and must find the one true raw instance, because the per-instance cache and the bound `this` of every method live on the raw. Three kinds of `this` arrive:

- **The raw object itself.** `toRaw` returns it unchanged, so the code reads the back-pointer. On the first ever access the pointer is missing and gets stamped as the object itself. Every later access is one `toRaw` read plus one symbol read.
- **A Vue reactive proxy.** `toRaw` sees through it via the `__v_raw` flag. The function returns the raw, stamping the pointer directly on the raw once. It deliberately never reads the pointer through the proxy, because a symbol read through a reactive proxy comes back deep-wrapped as `reactive(raw)` and also registers a dependency on that symbol inside any running effect. That wrapped value was the old poisoning bug: a method bound to it saw ref-unwrapping semantics, so `this.x.value` crashed.
- **A foreign proxy that does not answer `__v_raw`.** `toRaw` cannot help, so the pointer is read through the chain. It may come back wrapped, hence the `toRaw` normalization on the pointer. This is the branch the July fix added.

**Why this ordering is the correct one.** Pointer-first was the old shape, and it is faster on raw objects but routes every reactive-proxy access through a trap plus a wrap. I re-measured all three orderings just now, 2M ops each:

| input | current | inlined toRaw step | pointer-first |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| raw instance | 5.3 ns | 4.9 ns | 3.3 ns |
| reactive proxy | 28.4 ns | 25.8 ns | 56.8 ns |

Pointer-first doubles the reactive path, which matches the 37 to 48 percent the commit reported. The current order is the right trade.

**One correction to the mental model.** The commit message names Vue's component expose proxy as the case that needs the pointer fallback. I checked the Vue source: the expose proxy's inner layer is `proxyRefs`, whose get trap answers `__v_raw` with its target, and the outer layer calls `target[key]` so the receiver is that inner layer. So every Vue proxy is transparent to `toRaw`, including expose, readonly, and shallow variants. The pointer fallback only serves non-Vue proxies, and the regression test models that with a synthetic proxy that hides `__v_raw`. It is still worth keeping: it costs nothing on the two hot paths.

**The one corner that is not sound, and cannot be.** If an opaque foreign proxy is the very first thing to touch an instance, the last branch stamps the proxy as the raw through the proxy's set trap. I probed it: with a transparent opaque proxy everything keeps working but `this === instance` is false inside methods from then on. With an opaque proxy that also unwraps refs, it crashes the same way the original bug did. No Vue API produces either shape, and an opaque proxy is indistinguishable from a raw object from inside a prototype getter, so there is no structural fix. Not stamping in that branch does not help either, since the method would still bind to the proxy. It is a documented boundary, not a defect to chase.

**Can it be optimized further?** Only marginally. Inlining the first step of `toRaw` (read `__v_raw` yourself, recurse only when present) saves about 8 percent on both paths, roughly half a nanosecond raw and 2.5 ns through reactive, at the price of depending on Vue's flag string and about 20 more gzipped bytes against the 1.1 kB budget. The remaining cost on the reactive path is Vue's own get trap for `__v_raw`, which no ordering avoids. The raw path is already at its floor of two property reads: you cannot detect a proxy without one read, and you cannot find the raw without a second. My recommendation is to keep the current shape and spend the budget elsewhere, unless you want that 8 percent enough to accept the coupling.

The "cursor.ts" is `Caret.ts` in `app/src/ui/post-player/`, and the short answer is: swapping it for Tiptap is not a drop-in, because the player's editing model is the opposite of Tiptap's. It is doable, but the thing to replace is the item model, not the caret helper. **What the editor is today.** Each paragraph is its own `post_item` row with an `innerHTML` string body and a fractional `position`. Each row renders as a separate `contenteditable` span inside the virtual scroller. `Caret.ts` is a 200-line character-offset calculator over that span, and `PostPlayer.ts` does structural editing by hand: Enter on three trailing `
`s splits the DOM range into two rows, Backspace at offset zero merges rows behind a confirm dialog, paste rebuilds HTML from plain text, undo is a stub. Edits accumulate in `editState` (created, changed, removed) and save as one batch on the Save button. The search highlight and the seek promise both read the paragraph HTML string directly. **What Tiptap collaboration needs.** Tiptap's concurrent editing is the `Collaboration` and `CollaborationCursor` extensions over a Yjs document, synced by a websocket provider such as Hocuspocus or y-websocket. That assumes one ProseMirror document per editor instance, edits as CRDT operations rather than string replacements, and a server that relays Yjs updates and persists the Yjs state. The `realized` API has socket.io with a Redis adapter, but it is used only for room joins and WebRTC signalling. There is no Yjs anywhere and no document-state persistence. **Where the fit breaks.** - One Tiptap editor per paragraph row would give you thousands of editors under a virtual scroller. Rows mount and unmount as you scroll, so every row would need its own Yjs sub-document and provider. That is neither cheap nor what the extensions were built for. - One Tiptap document for the whole post is the natural Tiptap shape, but it dissolves the `post_item` table. Paragraph identity, fractional ordering, per-item media, numbering, and the scroller's item-based seek and search promises all key on rows. The invariants doc says the promise is an item, never a pixel. A single document has no items. - The batch save and the string-based search highlight would both need rewriting against ProseMirror state instead of HTML strings. **What transfers easily.** The app already ships Tiptap (`@tiptap/vue-3`, `starter-kit`, bubble menu, version 2.11) with a working `TiptapEditor.vue`, so the toolchain is in place. Paste, undo, and the split and merge heuristics would come for free from ProseMirror, which alone would delete most of `Caret.ts` and about 400 lines of `PostPlayer.ts`. **Options, ranked.** 1. **Hybrid, and my recommendation if collaboration is the goal.** Keep `post_item` rows as the unit of identity and give each row a Yjs `XmlFragment` inside one shared `Y.Doc` per post. Mount a Tiptap editor only for the focused row and render the rest as static HTML from the fragment. Presence cursors then show per row, split and merge become Yjs array operations on a shared item list, and the scroller contract survives untouched. Needs a Yjs relay on the API and Yjs state persistence beside the existing rows. Roughly a few weeks of work. 2. **Single document.** Cleanest Tiptap story, worst fit for the reader's player. You would rebuild seek, search, numbering, and media anchoring on ProseMirror node positions. 3. **Tiptap per row without collaboration.** Cheap and removes `Caret.ts`, but it buys none of the concurrent-editing capability you asked about. The plain fact underneath: Tiptap will not make this editor collaborative by itself. The collaboration lives in Yjs plus a relay server, and the real design decision is whether a paragraph stays a database row. Keeping it a row is what keeps the player's invariants intact.

The two background tasks are still the local dev servers, the vite dashboard on 5190 and the local Worker on 8787, kept up deliberately for the user. They are not stuck.

The goal itself is complete: every press-system checklist line is ticked and committed on `press-system` (`bd3ba1df`), including the R2 bucket the user enabled. Nothing remains for me; the merge, push, and production import are the user's calls. Leaving the servers running.

That direction fits Tiptap well, and the illusion you describe is cheaper to keep than it is today, because ProseMirror already knows where the caret is relative to the block. **The edge crossing.** `Caret.ts` exists to answer "is the caret on the first or last visual line" by counting characters. ProseMirror answers it directly: `view.endOfTextblock('down')` and `'up'` return true when a vertical move would leave the block, and they account for wrapped lines, which the character counter never did. So the per-item Tiptap extension binds ArrowUp and ArrowDown in `addKeyboardShortcuts`, asks that question, and when true hands focus to the neighbouring row. To keep the caret's horizontal position across the seam, read `view.coordsAtPos(selection.head).left` before leaving and place the new caret with `posAtCoords` in the next editor at that x, on its first or last line. ArrowLeft and ArrowRight at offset zero and end do the same with `'start'` and `'end'`. That is the whole of `Caret.ts`, reduced to four shortcuts. **One editor, moved between rows.** Do not create an editor per row. Keep one Tiptap `Editor` for the whole player and mount it into whichever row has focus: the row swaps its static `v-html` span for `EditorContent` bound to that editor, the editor gets the row's content, and on blur the row serializes back to its HTML body and returns to static rendering. Creation cost stops mattering, the bubble menu is one instance, and there is one keymap to reason about. Clear the history on each swap so undo never rewrites a previous paragraph. **The menu.** Tiptap's `BubbleMenu` is already the detached shape: it floats on the current selection and is owned by the editor, not the row, so the single shared editor carries a single menu that appears wherever the focus is. The existing `TiptapEditor.vue` in the app already wires it. If you meant a per-paragraph menu that stays put rather than following the selection, `FloatingMenu` anchored to the row wrapper covers that with the same extension family. **Split and merge become document operations.** Enter binds to a shortcut that cuts the document at the selection, keeps the head in the current row, and creates the next `post_item` with the tail as HTML. Backspace at position zero merges into the previous row by appending its content and moving the caret to the old boundary. The three-`
` heuristic and the confirm dialogs go away, and paste and undo come from ProseMirror for free. **What this leaves for collaboration later.** Because a paragraph stays a row, the Yjs step is additive: one `Y.Doc` per post, one `XmlFragment` per item id, and Tiptap's `Collaboration` extension takes that fragment through its `fragment` option when the editor mounts into a row. Remote cursors render inside the focused row through `CollaborationCursor`; for the other rows, the awareness state says which item each user is in, so a row-level presence mark is enough. The API side is a Yjs relay over the socket.io you already run plus persistence of the Yjs state next to the rows. The order I would build in: shared editor plus edge crossing first, which deletes `Caret.ts` and most of the split and merge code and is a self-contained change. Yjs second, once the row-level editor is stable, since it plugs into the same mount point.

was thinking undo should work across paragraphs though not forget on focusing next one

Agreed, and it changes where undo lives: it cannot be the focused editor's own history, because ProseMirror's history is a list of steps against one document, and after a row swap those steps point into the wrong text. Undo has to belong to the player, with the row editors as leaves.

**Before Yjs: keep the state, not the HTML.** When a row loses focus, do not throw its `EditorState` away and keep only the serialized body. Park the state on the item. The state carries the row's history branch and its selection, so refocusing the row with `view.updateState(parkedState)` brings back its undo stack intact, caret included. Untouched rows stay as HTML strings; only rows edited this session hold a state, so memory stays proportional to what was edited.

On top of that the player keeps one ordered log of undo targets: each row-level edit burst appends that row's id, and each structural operation (split, merge, move, remove) appends an entry that knows how to invert itself. Ctrl+Z then reads:

1. If the focused row's own history has depth, undo there. ProseMirror restores the text and the selection.
2. Otherwise pop the player log. A row entry focuses that row, restores its parked state, and undoes one step there, so the caret jumps to where the change was. A structural entry inverts itself: a split re-merges the two rows, a merge re-splits, a move restores the position.
3. Redo mirrors it with the same log walked forward.

The split case needs one rule so undo stays coherent: when Enter cuts a row, both resulting rows get a fresh history, and the split entry in the player log is the thing that undoes it. Otherwise the head row's old steps reference text that now lives in the tail row.

**After Yjs it collapses to one object.** With the post as a single `Y.Doc` holding one fragment per item plus the item order, a single `Y.UndoManager` over the whole doc tracks every local change across all paragraphs, structural operations included, because a split is just an array insert and two fragment edits in the same transaction. Tiptap's `Collaboration` extension swaps ProseMirror history for exactly that manager. Ctrl+Z in any row undoes the most recent local change wherever it happened, and the player only has to focus the row the undone change touched, which the manager reports in its `stack-item-popped` event. The parked-state log above is the pre-Yjs stand-in for that manager, so it is worth building it with the same shape: an ordered list of local changes, each knowing its row, so the swap later is a replacement and not a redesign.

One consequence worth deciding now: undo across paragraphs means Ctrl+Z can move the reader's viewport. The invariants doc says the reader owns the scroll, so the jump should use the same seek path as search, landing the row readable rather than snapping the caret to the edge.

Each row has an `innerHTML` string `body`, a fractional `position`, `numbered`, and optional media. The scroller's promises (an item, never a pixel; the reader owns the scroll) stay untouched. See `app/src/ui/virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller.invariants.md`. 2. **One Tiptap editor for the whole player, mounted into the focused row.** Not an editor per row. The focused row swaps its static `v-html` span for `EditorContent` bound to the shared editor; on blur the row serializes back to its HTML body and returns to static rendering. 3. **The one-editor illusion is kept by edge crossing**, answered by ProseMirror instead of by counting characters. 4. **Undo belongs to the player, not to the row editor.** It works across paragraphs and structural operations, and it is shaped so a Yjs `UndoManager` replaces it later without a redesign. 5. **The menu is the Tiptap bubble menu**, owned by the shared editor, so it follows the selection into whichever row has focus. 6. **Collaboration is additive**: one `Y.Doc` per post, one `XmlFragment` per item, relayed over the socket.io server that already exists. ## Design ### The shared editor - `PostEditor` (one class, the player owns it) creates a single Tiptap `Editor` with StarterKit (paragraph, text, hard break, marks the post needs, history), the bubble menu, and a `PostRow` extension carrying the keymap below. - Mounting: the focused `PostItem` renders `EditorContent` with the shared editor; the player loads the row's content on focus and takes the HTML back on blur. `editor.view.updateState(state)` swaps states, so a row with a parked state (see Undo) comes back with its history and caret. - The bubble menu shows on selection in the focused row. If the focused row's own history has depth, undo there. ProseMirror restores text and selection. 2. Otherwise pop the log. A row entry focuses that row, restores its parked state and undoes one step. A structural entry inverts itself: a split re-merges, a merge re-splits, a move restores the position. 3. Redo walks the same log forward. - **Split rule**: both rows produced by a split get a fresh history; the split entry in the player log is what undoes the split. Otherwise the head row's old steps would reference text now living in the tail. - **The jump respects the reader.** Undo that lands in another paragraph moves the viewport through the same seek path search uses, landing the row readable, never snapping the caret to the edge. ### Save Unchanged in this phase: rows serialize to HTML on blur and flow into `editState`; the Save button batches them as today. It reduces cleanly, and the reduction is the point: the scroller never needs to know about hierarchy.

**What the scroller actually requires.** One flat list of items, each with an identity and a measured height. It already handles variable heights. Nothing in it cares what is inside a row. So a full-width section row with a heading, three columns and an image is, to the scroller, one item with one height, exactly like a paragraph today.

**So hierarchy lives in the data, not in the scroller.** Keep `post_item` flat in the database with a `parent_id` and the same fractional `position` scoped to the parent. Root rows are the scroller's items. A container row renders its children as ordinary DOM inside itself, recursively. Children are still rows, so they keep identity, per-item media, search hits, and the focused-leaf editor from the plan. The scroller virtualizes roots only, which is what a website builder wants anyway: sections scroll, the inside of a section is a layout.

**What that buys for the editor plan without changes.**

- The shared Tiptap editor still mounts into one focused leaf. A container is never edited as text; its leaves are.
- Edge crossing generalizes from "next row" to "next leaf in document order", a depth-first walk over the tree. Same four shortcuts.
- The undo log already keys on row ids. Structural entries gain two verbs, move-into and move-out-of a container, and everything else holds.
- Yjs maps onto it as one `Y.Map` of items by id with a parent pointer and a per-parent `Y.Array` of child ids, or a nested tree of arrays. The flat map is easier to merge and matches the table.

**Where the hard part really is.** Three places, none of them the nesting itself:

- **The item promise.** Seek and search promise an item lands readable. For a child, the landing target is its root row, offset by the child's position inside it. That is the same `innerFraction` idea search already uses for a match inside a paragraph, one level up.
- **Giant containers.** A section with a thousand children is one un-virtualized row. Cap the depth and child count a container may hold, or promote such a container to a run of root rows. The rule can be simple: containers hold layout, not lists.
- **Layout kinds.** A container needs a `layout` field (stack, columns, grid) and the renderer for each. That is builder work, not scroller work, and it is where the effort goes.

The simple case you describe, a div with sub-parts, is just a container row with `layout: stack`, and it is all the plan needs to be ready for.

Agreed on both: the book player stays flat, and nesting is the site designer's problem.

The chat demo is a good fit, and the scroller already has most of what a chat list needs. It measures rendered items through a ResizeObserver and re-prefixes heights on every burst, so a last message growing token by token is the normal case, not a special one. Bottom-clamped positioning and `scrollToIndex` exist. What a chat surface adds on top is small and specific:

- **Stick to bottom while streaming, release the moment the reader scrolls up.** That is one rule on top of the existing clamp, and it is the same "the reader owns the scroll" invariant the post player already states.
- **Prepend older history without a jump.** Loading earlier messages above the viewport must keep the visible message where it is. The scroller's "identity survives, pixels don't" invariant is exactly the property that makes this cheap: re-anchor on the item, not on scrollTop.
- **Variable, late-settling heights.** Code blocks with syntax highlighting and images that load after mount are the chat-specific stress on measurement, and the demo should include them on purpose.

What makes it a selling point rather than a toy is the receipt. Most chat UIs, including some well-known ones, render the whole thread in the DOM and stall past a few thousand messages. A demo that holds a 10,000-message conversation with streaming replies, code blocks, and instant jump to any message, with the DOM node count shown live next to the message count, says the thing without saying it. It is also the kind of page a reader keeps open, which is what the site wants.

The one constraint is the model. The site is static, so the demo streams a canned conversation, or a scripted generator that produces plausible long replies, clearly labelled. That is fine: the claim is about the list, not the model, and a fake stream is more honest for a benchmark than a live key would be.

Shape-wise it is an ivue class owning the thread, the stream, and the anchor rule, with the scroller underneath, which also makes it a second worked example of the standard beside the post player. When you want it built, it belongs in the ivue repo as an examples page plus a short post with the numbers.

Both answers, from the code as it stands.

**Selection over arbitrary HTML.** The selection is logical: an item index plus a character offset into that row's text. The pointer is resolved with `caretPositionFromPoint`, which lands in any DOM, so highlighting and dragging work over whatever a row contains: bold, links, code spans, images. The limit is in what "the row's text" means. A mounted row's text is `textContent` trimmed, and an unmounted row's text is whatever the `selectionText` prop returns for the item. Two consequences for a chat message:

- **Inline HTML is fully supported today.** Offsets walk the text nodes in order, and `textContent` of inline markup is the visible string.
- **Block HTML copies without block separators.** `textContent` of two paragraphs or a list has no newline between the blocks, so a copied message would glue paragraphs together. Code blocks survive because their newlines are real text nodes. Fixing this is one contained change in the selection class: measure and copy against `innerText`, which is layout-aware, instead of `textContent`, and keep the offset walk consistent with it. The invariant "the copied text is the string the row renders" stays true, it just becomes true for blocks too.
- **Copy is plain text only.** The clipboard gets `text/plain` assembled from the data across mounted and unmounted rows. That is what chats copy anyway. Adding `text/html` would mean slicing HTML at character offsets and is not worth it for the demo.

The one rule the chat class must honour: its `selectionText(item)` projection must produce exactly the mounted row's rendered text, or a copy that crosses the window boundary changes wording halfway. So the markdown renderer and the text projection are two views of one function, and the demo should test that they agree on every message.

**On-demand loading.** The scroller's contract with the data is minimal and that is what makes this easy: it reads `items.length` for the count and `items[index]` for a row, and an unmeasured row costs the running average height. It never needs the item's content to place it. So loading belongs in the chat class, not in the scroller:

- The class asks the mock API for the thread's message count first, then hands the scroller an array of that length filled with stubs, each carrying only its id and a pending flag.
- It watches the scroller's rendered window, which is already reactive, and fetches the pages that cover the window plus a margin, replacing stubs in place. Identity survives, so rows above the viewport do not move when a page lands.
- A stub renders as a placeholder sized to the scroller's current estimated item size. That is the one rule that keeps the fetch from disturbing the geometry: a placeholder measured at the average does not move the average, so the scrollbar and the seek stay stable while pages arrive.

The scroller needs nothing new for this beyond exposing the estimated size, which it already computes. The demo makes the point visible by showing the request log and the bytes transferred next to the message count: a 30 MB thread, a few hundred kilobytes fetched, whichever page the reader is on.

Both pieces are the same shape as the post player: an ivue class owning the data and the rules, the scroller underneath owning only geometry.

# AI chat on the virtual scroller

A long-context chat example for ivue.dev: a conversation of tens of
thousands of messages that streams replies, loads its history on demand,
jumps anywhere instantly, and copies cleanly, on top of the playground's
`VirtualScroller` with an ivue class owning everything above geometry.

Status: plan. Nothing here is built yet.

## Why

Most chat interfaces render the whole thread into the DOM and load the
whole thread as one JSON body. Past a few thousand messages both stall.
The scroller already solves the first; the chat class solves the second.
The page states the receipt live: messages in the thread, rows in the
DOM, bytes fetched so far. It is also a worked example of a dependency
between two ivue classes (chat over scroller), beside the post player.

## What exists

- `examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller.ts`:
  variable heights measured through a ResizeObserver, prefix sums over
  measured-or-assumed sizes, a running average for unmeasured rows
  (`estimatedItemSize`), bottom clamp, `scrollToIndex`, a reactive
  rendered window (`visibleItems`, `visibleIndex`).
- `VirtualScrollerSelection.ts`: a logical selection over the data
  (item index + character offset), highlight re-pinned on mounted rows,
  copy assembled from every row in the range through `rowText(index)`:
  the mounted row's DOM, or the `selectionText` prop for unmounted rows.
  Copy emits `text/plain` only. Specs: `docs_v2/examples/virtual-scroller-specs.md`,
  invariants beside the code.
- The docs site is static. No model runs behind it.

## Decisions

1. **Loading lives in the chat class, not in the scroller.** The
   scroller's contract with data is `items.length` and `items[index]`;
   it never needs content to place a row. Nothing is added to it for
   loading.
2. **Unloaded messages are stubs sized to the estimated item size.** A
   placeholder measured at the running average does not move the
   average, so pages arriving never move the scrollbar or the seek.
3. **The reader owns the scroll.** Stick to bottom only while the reader
   is at the bottom; release on the first upward scroll; a "jump to
   latest" chip brings it back. Same invariant as the post player.
4. **History prepends without a jump**, anchored on item identity, never
   on scrollTop.
5. **The stream is scripted, and says so.** A generator yields plausible
   replies token by token with realistic latency, markdown, code blocks,
   and the odd image. The claim is about the list, not the model.
6. **Selection measures and copies against rendered text, blocks
   included.** One contained change in the selection class: `innerText`
   instead of `textContent` for the row's text and the offset walk, so a
   copied message keeps its paragraph breaks. Plain text stays the only
   clipboard format.
7. **The chat's text projection is the renderer's twin.** `selectionText(message)`
   must return exactly the mounted row's rendered text, or a copy that
   crosses the window boundary changes wording halfway. Tested per
   message kind.

## Design

### `Chat` (ivue class, owns the thread)

- State: `total` (message count from the API), `items` (a shallow array
  of length `total`; stubs `{ id, pending: true }` until loaded),
  `pages` loaded, `streaming` message, `atBottom`, request log, bytes.
- Watches the scroller's rendered window and fetches the pages covering
  it plus a margin of one page each side. Replaces stubs in place. Never
  fetches a page twice; in-flight pages are remembered.
- Streaming: appends a message, then grows its body from the generator.
  The scroller remeasures the growing row on its own; the class only
  re-asserts the bottom while `atBottom`.
- Prepend: when the reader reaches the top of the loaded range, loads
  the previous page. Items before the viewport are replaced in place by
  index, so identity holds and nothing visible moves.
- `selectionText(message)`: the plain-text projection of the rendered
  markdown, with block boundaries as newlines. The same function feeds
  the renderer's text nodes, so the two cannot drift.
- Receipts as getters: `domRowCount`, `bytesFetched`, `requestCount`,
  `messageCount`, shown in a header strip.

### `ChatApi` (the mock, a class with statics)

- `count(threadId)`, `page(threadId, index, size)` with a latency model
  (jitter, an occasional slow page) and a byte size per page so the
  transfer counter is honest. Deterministic from a seed, so the demo
  reads the same every visit and the tests are reproducible.
- `stream(prompt)`: an async generator of tokens with per-token delay.

### Message rendering

- Kinds: user, assistant, system; bodies in the markdown subset the
  press already renders (paragraphs, lists, quotes, code fences, inline
  code, links, images). Code blocks highlighted with shiki at render.
- A stub renders as a placeholder at exactly the estimated item size.
- Images carry width and height, so a late load never remeasures.

### Selection changes (in the scroller's selection class)

- `rowText(row)` and `leadingWhitespaceLength` move to `innerText`; the
  offset walk stays over text nodes but block boundaries count one
  newline, matching `innerText`.
- The invariant "the copied text is the string the row renders" gains
  the block case in `virtual-scroller.invariants.md`, with a test that
  copies across a paragraph break and a code fence.

### Page and post

- `docs_v2/examples/ai-chat.md` with the live demo and the receipts
  strip; source tabs through `LazyCodeGroup`.
- A blog post per the write-article skill, title first, with the
  measured numbers: thread size, DOM rows, bytes fetched to read a
  given page, time to jump from first to last message.

## Order of work

1. `ChatApi` mock with the latency and byte model; unit tests.
2. `Chat` class over the scroller: stubs, window-driven paging, prepend
   without jump, stick-to-bottom rule; unit tests with a fake scroller.
3. Streaming replies and the growing last row.
4. Selection: `innerText` change, block-boundary offsets, tests; the
   `selectionText` twin test per message kind.
5. The example page, the receipts strip, a screenshot in both themes.
6. Measurements and the post.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] A 50,000-message thread opens with one count request and one
      page; the DOM holds only the rendered window plus overscan.
- [ ] Scrolling anywhere fetches only the pages covering the window;
      no page is fetched twice; the request log shows it.
- [ ] Pages arriving above the viewport do not move the visible message
      by a pixel (measured, not eyeballed).
- [ ] A streaming reply keeps the bottom pinned while the reader is at
      the bottom and stops pinning on the first upward scroll.
- [ ] Jump to message N from either end lands it readable in one seek.
- [ ] Copy across two paragraphs, a list, and a code fence keeps the
      breaks; copy across the window boundary reads the same as a copy
      inside it.
- [ ] `selectionText` equals the rendered row text for every message
      kind in the fixture thread.
- [ ] The scroller's own test suite and invariants check pass unchanged
      apart from the block-text invariant added on purpose.
- [ ] `npm run build:docs` passes; the page renders in both themes.

## Impossibilities (what this design forbids)

- A request for a page the window does not need.
- A placeholder whose measured height differs from the estimated size.
- A copy whose text differs between a mounted and an unmounted row.
- A programmatic bottom-pin that fights a reader scrolling up.
- The scroller knowing that a row is unloaded.

**Tool-call batches.** The parser groups any run of two or more tool calls with no text or thinking between them into a `tool_batch` part. # Virtual scroller: 1,000,000 rows on Lenis

A virtualized list where **scrolling itself is virtual**: a customized
[Lenis](https://github.com/darkroomengineering/lenis) drives the position
over `translateY` instead of native scroll, so momentum, touch feel and
wheel behavior are owned by code — while the DOM holds only the visible
window between two spacer `div`s. Heights are estimated until rows are
seen, captured one-shot as rows enter and leave, and every operation stays
O(window): nothing ever costs O(total items).

The class is a single ivue `Reactive()` unit — template refs, prop refs,
scroll state, the windowing math and the Lenis lifecycle all live on one
instance, constructed in `setup()` and torn down by the component scope.

</ClientOnly>

```vue

import VirtualScroller from './virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller.vue'
import type { VirtualScroller as Scroller } from './virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller'

const items = ref<Scroller.BaseItem[]>(loadRows()) // any size — 1M is routine
</script>

<template>
  <VirtualScroller v-model="items" :assumed-size="56" :padding-quantity="10">
    <template #item="{ item }">
      <article>{{ item.body }}</article>
    </template>
  </VirtualScroller>
</template>
```

Findings.

## 1. Playground registration and routing

- `~/dev/ivue/examples/playground/src/examples/index.ts` — the single registry. Each example folder ships a `manifest.ts`; the index imports it and adds one entry with a lazy `load`:
  ```ts
  import { manifest as virtualScroller } from './virtual-scroller/manifest';
  ...
  { ...virtualScroller, load: () => import('./virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerExample.vue') },
  ```
  Entry type: `{ slug, title, blurb, docsPath, load }`. Comment in the file is binding: "ORDER MATTERS — this list drives the playground sidebar and must stay in the SAME order as the docs sidebar (Basic → Advanced)". Quasar routes wrap `load` with `withQuasar(...)`; nothing else installs Quasar.
- `~/dev/ivue/examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/manifest.ts` — 5 fields only: `slug: 'virtual-scroller'`, `title`, `blurb`, `docsPath: '/examples/virtual-scroller'`.
- Routing/menu: `~/dev/ivue/examples/playground/src/App.vue` renders `playground.examples` as sidebar buttons and mounts `<component :is="playground.activeComponent" :key="playground.activeSlug" />`; logic in `~/dev/ivue/examples/playground/src/Playground.ts`. No vue-router.
- Folder layout of `examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/`:
  - classes: `VirtualScroller.ts`, `VirtualScrollerItem.ts`, `VirtualScrollerSelection.ts`, `VirtualScrollerSelectionTouch.ts`, `VirtualScrollerPadding.ts`, `HorizontalVirtualScroller.ts`, `VirtualScrollerExample.ts`
  - SFCs: `VirtualScroller.vue`, `VirtualScrollerItem.vue`, `VirtualScrollerTrack.vue`, `HorizontalVirtualScroller.vue`, `VirtualScrollerExample.vue` (the playground route component)
  - specs: `X.test.ts` colocated beside each `X.ts`, plus the test harness `hosted.ts` (mounts a throwaway component so constructor lifecycle hooks register)
  - contract: `virtual-scroller.invariants.md`
  - `manifest.ts`

## 2. docs_v2 live embed

- Wrapper component: `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/examples/ExampleVirtualScroller.vue`. It imports the playground files by relative path (not the alias) and constructs the playground's own class:
  ```ts
  import DemoBox from '../DemoBox.vue';
  import VirtualScroller from '../../../../../examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller.vue';
  import { VirtualScrollerExample } from '../../../../../examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerExample';
  const example = new VirtualScrollerExample.Class();
  ```
  It wraps content in `<DemoBox title note>`; only the chrome is docs code.
- Page usage: `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/examples/virtual-scroller.md` — frontmatter `title/description/aside: false/pageClass: benchmarks-wide examples-page/relatedPosts: [...]`, a `<script setup>` importing `LazyCodeGroup` and `ExampleVirtualScroller`, then `<ClientOnly><ExampleVirtualScroller /></ClientOnly>`.
- Specs page: `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/examples/virtual-scroller-specs.md` — prose plus two `LazyCodeGroup` blocks listing the `*.test.ts` files and the `.invariants.md` contract.
- Index listing: `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/examples/index.md`, inside `## Full-complexity` → `<div class="ix-example-list">` bullet list.
- Vite alias, `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/.vitepress/config.ts:145-156`:
  ```ts
  resolve: { dedupe: ['vue'], alias: { '@examples': fileURLToPath(new URL('../../examples/playground/src/examples', import.meta.url)) } },
  server: { fs: { allow: ['../..'] } }
  ```
- LazyCodeGroup syntax (repo-relative paths, no import of the source):
  ```md
  <LazyCodeGroup
    :files="[
        { path: 'examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller.ts', label: 'VirtualScroller.ts' },
        { path: 'docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/examples/ExampleVirtualScroller.vue', label: 'template' }
    ]"
  />
  ```
  Component: `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/LazyCodeGroup.vue` + `LazyCodeGroup.ts`. Backed by `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/.vitepress/plugins/lazy-source.mjs`, registered in config as `plugins: [lazySourcePlugin()]`. It enumerates files under `ROOTS = ['examples/playground/src', 'docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/examples']` and highlights each with shiki into its own chunk (`virtual:lazy-source-map`, `lazy-source:<path>`). A new example under those roots is picked up automatically.

## 3. VirtualScroller public surface

`~/dev/ivue/examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScroller.vue`:
```ts
const props = defineProps(VirtualScroller.Class.props) as unknown as VirtualScroller.Props<T>;
const emit = defineEmits(VirtualScroller.Class.emits) as VirtualScroller.Emits;
defineSlots<VirtualScroller.Slots<T>>();
const virtualScroller = new VirtualScroller.Class<T>(props, emit);
defineExpose(virtualScroller as VirtualScroller.Instance<T>);
```
Props declared as statics in `VirtualScroller.ts` (`static get propsTypes()` at line 65, defaults merged separately; `Props<T>` derived by `ExtractPropTypes` at line 1980): `modelValue` (required `BaseItem[]`), `scrollbar`, `autoPlay`, `autoPlayDelay`, `autoRepeat`, `snapToItems`, `snapAlign: 'start'|'center'`, `assumedSize`, `paddingQuantity`, `creepMsPerPx`, `scroll` (nested motion knobs), `selection` (nested autoscroll knobs), `draggable`, `selectionText: (item) => string`, `selectionJoin`, `dragHandleSelector`, `dragClass`, `dragGhostClass`, `dragChosenClass`.

Emits (`static get emits()`, line 152): `itemsChanged(args: ItemsChangeEmitArgs)`, `drop(startIndex, dropIndex)`, `move(event)`.

Slot: one, `item`, scope `ItemContext<T> = { item: T; id: string; index: number }` (line 2020).

Consumer type: `VirtualScroller.Exposed<T> = ShallowUnwrapRef<Instance<T>>` (line 2037).

Public members a parent uses: `scrollToIndex(index, afterCallback?, animate = true, topOffsetPx = snapAlignOffset(index), innerFraction = 0)` (line 1546), `startAutoPlay(delay)`, `stopAutoPlay()`, `isAutoPlaying`, `visibleItems`, `visibleIndex {start,end}` (line 590), `estimatedItemSize` (line 585, `calibratedAssumed ?? assumedSize`), `selection` (with `selectedRowCount`, `copy()`, event handlers), `scrollPosition`, `scrollExtent`, `containerSize`, `scrollElement`/`itemsWrapperElement`, `leadingSpacerPx`/`trailingSpacerPx`. There is no `scrollToEnd`; the bottom clamp lives in `setScrollPosition` and `lenis.virtualLimit` (lines 300-306), and "jump to end" is done by index.

Post-player usage in `~/dev/ivue/examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerExample.ts`:
```ts
get scroller() { return ref<VirtualScroller.Exposed<VirtualScroller.BaseItem> | null>(null); }
get renderedCount() { return this.scroller.value?.visibleItems.length ?? 0; }
get isAutoPlaying() { return this.scroller.value?.isAutoPlaying ?? false; }
get selectedRowCount() { return this.scroller.value?.selection.selectedRowCount ?? 0; }
jumpTo(index) { this.scroller.value?.scrollToIndex(index, undefined, true, 12); }
jumpToEnd() { this.jumpTo(this.itemCount - 1); }
toggleAutoPlay() { ... scroller.stopAutoPlay() : scroller.startAutoPlay(0) }
rowText(item) { return `#${Number(row.position).toLocaleString()} — ${row.body}`; }  // passed as :selection-text
```
Template binding (both the playground SFC and the docs wrapper): `ref="scroller" scrollbar v-model="items" :assumed-size="56" :padding-quantity="10" :creep-ms-per-px :selection-text="example.rowText" auto-play :auto-play-delay="800"` with `<template #item="{ item }">`.

## 4. Tests and docs plumbing

- One root config runs playground specs: `~/dev/ivue/vitest.config.ts` — `environment: 'jsdom'`, positive `include` with `"examples/**/*.test.ts"`, `dedupe` of every `@vue/*` package, `server.deps.inline: ['@vue/test-utils','@vueuse/core','@vueuse/shared','vue-demi']`. `examples/playground/vite.config.ts` has no test block; `examples/playground/package.json` has no test script. Run from the repo root (`npm test` / `vitest run`).
- Spec header form (first 30 lines of `VirtualScrollerSelection.test.ts`): a `=== GENERATOR ===` block with `Goal:`, then markdown links to anchors in `virtual-scroller.invariants.md`, then `// domain-invariant: $Class — If … then …` lines, then `Impossible if true:` lines. The invariants checker binds these to the sibling contract.
- Sidebar: `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/.vitepress/config.ts` lists examples TWICE (lines ~753-758 and ~817-822 — two sidebar sets), under `text: 'Full Complexity'`, e.g. `{ text: 'Virtual Scroller: 1M Items', link: '/examples/virtual-scroller' }` and `{ text: 'Virtual Scroller: Specs', link: '/examples/virtual-scroller-specs' }`. Both must be edited.
- OG images: `transformHead({ pageData })` at config.ts:540 builds og:title/description/url from frontmatter, and looks for `docs_v2/public/og/<relativePath with / → ->.png` (so `examples/ai-chat.md` → `docs_v2/public/og/examples-ai-chat.png`); if absent it falls back to `https://ivue.dev/og-image.png`. Generator: `npm run render:page-og` → `docs_v2/scripts/page-og-generator.mjs`.
- `npm run build:docs` chains `gate:docs` (`scripts/gate-docs.mjs`), `sync:examples` (`scripts/sync-examples.mjs` — copies `lib/Reactive.ts|nestedProps.ts|clone.ts` into the playground so StackBlitz is self-contained), then `check:links` and `check-related-posts.mjs`. A new docs page with `relatedPosts` frontmatter is checked by the latter.

## 5. shiki and markdown availability

- shiki is used only at build time by `~/dev/ivue/docs_v2/.vitepress/plugins/lazy-source.mjs` (`import { codeToHtml } from 'shiki'`) and by VitePress's own markdown highlighter (`markdown: { theme: { light: 'github-light', dark: 'one-dark-pro' } }`, config.ts:577). It is a transitive vitepress dependency — not declared in root or `docs_v2` package.json, and NOT used anywhere in `examples/playground/src`. No runtime shiki in any theme component: an in-page runtime highlighter would need a new dependency (or a build-time route through the lazy-source plugin).
- No markdown renderer in the playground. `grep -rn 'markdown'` over `examples/playground/src` matches only a comment in `VirtualScrollerSelection.ts` and `flyweight-grid/RESULTS.md`. No `marked` / `markdown-it` / `highlight.js` in root or `docs_v2` package.json. Playground deps are `@vueuse/core`, `vue`, `fast-formula-parser`, `quasar`, `@quasar/extras` only — an ai-chat example rendering markdown must either add a dependency to `examples/playground/package.json` (which also affects the StackBlitz boot) or ship its own minimal renderer class.
